resources.string: Pipeline Builder
Build displays, toys and your own controls. Follow the guided editor tours at your own pace.
Canvas and blocks
Events and state
Design your Ambient
Create a toy
Reuse your work
Build your own controls and menus
Use custom controls safely
Inspect and share
Tutorial project
This is the same editor you use for your own pipelines. This tour uses a temporary project. Nothing is saved or sent to your Glyph.
Drag empty canvas space to move in either direction. Pinch to zoom. Recenter brings your blocks back into view.
An event starts a stack of blocks. This stack runs when the pipeline starts.
Choose a display block and drop it inside the event. Blocks run in order from top to bottom.
Control blocks contain other blocks. Here a repeat block runs the display and wait together. Drop markers show exactly where a block will go.
Select a block to change its inputs. Inputs have types and units: this wait is a duration in milliseconds.
Undo and Redo work on complete edits. Moving around the canvas does not add undo steps.
Preview runs the actual pipeline with sample inputs. You can send a key press without using the phone’s real button.
Save draft keeps work in progress. Apply checks the whole project before replacing its running revision. A broken draft does not interrupt a working pipeline.
An event is something that happens once. A condition describes what is true now. A key press is an event; music playing is a condition.
If chooses one of two paths. Combine conditions with All, Any or Not. Unavailable sensor data stays unavailable; it is not treated as zero.
Variables remember values between events. Here a press increases a counter. A variable belongs to its project or routine, unless you explicitly make it persistent.
Repeat runs a fixed number of times. Forever repeats until its owner stops. Wait yields execution so other events can still respond.
A random expression can choose a value within a range. Preview starts with a fixed seed so the same demonstration can be replayed.
A named timer can be restarted. Each press moves this deadline forward, so the timeout counts from the most recent press.
Cancel the timer by name when it is no longer needed. Stopping a project also removes its temporary listeners and work.
An Ambient pipeline runs as the background toy. It controls what appears there while the standard toy menu remains available.
Build a cycle from the displays you want. Their order here is their order on Glyph. A press can move to the next display.
Expose the interval as a quick setting. It becomes available in Ambient settings without reopening the block canvas.
Charging and music can have higher priority than the background cycle. Only the winning presentation draws; the background can keep its place.
A press can temporarily hide the music presentation and return to the background. A named timeout controls when music may return.
Press again before the timeout to restart it. The return time is measured from the latest press, not the first one.
Apply saves the valid revision. Use for Ambient assigns it to the background toy. Its declared quick settings appear in the Ambient settings popup.
A toy pipeline is a new selectable toy. It starts when selected or called by another pipeline. Adding it to Toys does not play or enable it automatically.
Use a design from your library or draw one in the existing design editor. Designs supply frames and animations; blocks decide when they run.
Artwork opens in the same Custom Design Editor. Draw and adjust your frames here, then return them to the pipeline’s draft. The demonstration stays in this temporary sandbox.
React to a press with a display or animation. Add variables and loops when your toy needs state that changes over time.
Built-in originals are read-only. Make a copy to change settings, artwork or behavior while keeping the original available.
A native Dino block supplies the game’s movement and collisions. Its jump artwork slot can use your own animation without replacing that behavior.
Choose how an animation fits its phase. Crop, anchor and hitbox are separate: changing the picture does not have to change where collisions occur.
Review both matrix sizes. Artwork uses a separate variant for each panel. Missing artwork is reported; it is never stretched silently.
Turn a useful stack into a named routine. Call it from several places instead of maintaining separate copies.
Parameters let each call supply a different input. Here the routine accepts how long its display should stay visible.
These two events call the same routine with different arguments. Renaming the routine does not break either call.
A routine may return a typed result. Its local variables belong to that call; project variables are shared by that project’s handlers.
Projects keep explicit copies of routine revisions. Updating a library routine does not unexpectedly change a running project. Update references and Apply when ready.
Export includes referenced routines, designs and settings. The receiving device gets a complete inactive copy, with fresh local identities.
Custom controls and menus let you decide how Glyph responds and navigates. Your controller supplies its own menu instead of using the Toys selector.
A selected-index variable remembers the menu item. A press changes the index; modulo wraps the last item back to the first.
Draw the selected item using frames, text or a called routine. Your menu can look and behave however you design it.
A confirm event calls the selected toy. Define the return event too, so the user can get back to the menu.
Global rules can temporarily take priority. For example, face down shows Clock, or a shake shows Weather for 30 seconds.
When an interruption ends, resume the previous menu or toy. Preview makes both the active presentation and hidden branches visible.
Saving or applying a controller never enables custom controls by itself. Activation is available only in App settings, where you can also stop it.
Custom controls are enabled only from App settings. Choose a valid controller, review its required capabilities and configure pocket protection.
While custom controls are enabled, Toys is unavailable. Your controller owns the menu and navigation. Create, Settings and Tutorials remain available.
Stop is outside the pipeline’s control. It stops a faulty or unwanted controller even if that controller has no working menu.
Return to Standard restores normal toy selection. Editing and previewing a controller never changes this mode without your choice.
Pause preview to inspect a moment. Step advances the same interpreter used on Glyph; it does not play a separate mock animation.
A waiting block remains visible in the trace. Inspect its variables and timer, or advance time to see what happens next.
A higher-priority display can hide another branch without deleting its state. Inspect the presentation list to see why a branch is hidden.
Validation points to incomplete inputs and broken references. Fix this wait’s missing duration before applying the project.
The portable glyph.pipeline JSON file includes the required programs, routines, artwork and native capabilities. It excludes sensor readings, permissions and running state.
You can replay this chapter at any time. Use a starter in the pipeline library when you want to make your own version.
